# Purpose
This project examines overall trends in CTA L ridership between 1999 and 2024 and identifies how the COVID-19 pandemic may have influenced train travel--both generally and across specific lines (e.g., Green, Pink, Red) and neighborhood categories--in the City of Chicago throughout the various waves of the pandemic. The sections below step you through the process for creating tables, maps and figures to inform your presentation. *As with previous exercises, you are asked to combine and submit all materials into a single presentation. The basic template for this exercise can be downloaded [via this link to the PowerPoint slides](https://justenvirons.org/pedagogy/GEO330/Exercise_03/slides/Exercise03_Template.pptx) on the course data pages.*

The load command imports the datasets listed below, along with custom functions (all beginning with "fx_") that create the exercise's tables, plots and maps. The code for each function can be viewed by clicking the "Show" links throughout this document.

- `community_areas_ccvi`: City of Chicago community areas with COVID-19 Community Vulnerability Index (CCVI) scores, categories and ranks
- `rail_stations`: CTA L stations in Chicago with their line and nearest community area and zip code

- `rail_stations_ccvi_ridership`: monthly weekday boardings by L station, with station line and CCVI
- `covid19_cases_summary`: daily COVID-19 cases and deaths in Chicago (daily, 7-day average and cumulative)

# Step 2. Explore geographic data 
This exercise evaluates L ridership and COVID-19 trends for neighborhoods in the city of Chicago. To do this, we need community areas, zip codes and L stations in a spatial (i.e., mappable) format. These datasets, and all data for this exercise, are publicly available via the [Chicago data portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org/) and the Regional Transportation Authority's Mapping and Statistics [(RTAMS)](https://rtams.org/) websites. CTA rail stations and lines were downloaded from the *Shapefiles and Feature Layers* section of the [RTAMS Maps and Data web page](https://rtagis.maps.arcgis.com/home/index.html).

## L stations by community area and zip code
It is necessary to attribute L stations with community areas and zip codes in order to evaluate CCVI and COVID-19 cases with ridership trends. That is, ridership is reported by L station whereas CCVI and COVID-19 cases are reported by community area and zip code. Therefore each L station in the `rail_stations` dataset was associated with its nearest community area and zip code using a spatial join. @fig-stationbycomareazip below tabulates L stations by community area and zip code.

```{r}
#| label: define station table functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the station table functions"

# function for formatting a table as an interactive table
fx_datatable <- function(table) {
  datatable(table,
            class = 'cell-border stripe',
            rownames = FALSE,
            options = list(pageLength = 5),
            filter = "top")
}

# function for tabulating L stations by community area and zip code
fx_table_stations <- function(rail_stations) {
  rail_stations %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(`L Station` = station_name,
           `Community Area` = comarea_name,
           `Station Line` = station_line,
           `Zip Code` = zip) %>%
    arrange(`L Station`) %>%
    fx_datatable()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-stationbycomareazip
#| fig-cap: L Station by Community Area and Zip Code

# tabulate L stations by community area and zip code
fx_table_stations(rail_stations)

```

## CCVI by Chicago community area
We will be evaluating L ridership based on a variety of community characteristics included in the Chicago COVID-19 Community Vulnerability Index (CCVI). The index was adapted and modified from [Surgo Ventures](https://precisionforcovid.org/ccvi) and the [CDC Social Vulnerability Index](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/placeandhealth/svi/index.html) to identify communities (i.e., both community areas and zip codes) in Chicago that have been disproportionately impacted by COVID-19. Vulnerability is defined as a combination of: sociodemographic factors; epidemiological factors; occupational factors and other factors related to cumulative COVID burden. These factors are combined and weighted to create a single composite CCVI score. The higher the score, the more vulnerable the geographic area or, in this case, community area. The `community_areas_ccvi` dataset joins the CCVI scores, categories and ranks (from least (1) to most (77) vulnerable) to community areas.

## Create map showing CCVI distribution by community area 
R has several packages devoted to map making. The *leaflet* package can be used to create custom, interactive maps (@fig-ccvibycommunityarea). Modify the color palette ([see this reference for palette names](https://i0.wp.com/1.bp.blogspot.com/-3VQwNXWga9s/UICXF7rbvLI/AAAAAAAAAUg/UQBmpUO9kVA/s1600/display-brewer-all.png)) in the code below to create a custom map showing variations by CCVI category. Insert the map into slide 1 of your presentation.

```{r}
#| label: define CCVI mapping function
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the CCVI mapping function"

# function for mapping CCVI category by community area; palette is any
# RColorBrewer palette name (e.g., "YlOrRd", "Blues", "PuRd")
fx_map_ccvi <- function(community_areas_ccvi, palette = "YlOrRd") {
  map_data <- st_transform(community_areas_ccvi, crs = 4326)

  map_pal <- colorFactor(palette = palette,
                         domain = map_data$`CCVI Category`,
                         ordered = TRUE)

  # hover labels
  labels <- sprintf(
    "<strong>%s</strong><br/>
    <i>CCVI Score:</i> %0.1f<br/>
    <i>CCVI Category:</i> %s<br/><br/>
    <em>Ranked scores from least (1) to most (77) vulnerable:</em><br/>
    <ul style=\"list-style-type:square;\">
    <li>Socioeconomic Status: %1.0f</li>
    <li>Essential Workers: %1.0f</li>
    <li>Mobility Ratio: %1.0f</li>
    <li>COVID-19 Incidence Rate: %1.0f</li>
    <li>COVID-19 Hospitalization Rate: %1.0f</li>
    <li>COVID-19 Crude Mortality Rate: %1.0f</li>",
    map_data$comarea_name,
    map_data$`CCVI Score`,
    map_data$`CCVI Category`,
    map_data$`Rank - Socioeconomic Status`,
    map_data$`Rank - Frontline Essential Workers`,
    map_data$`Rank - Cumulative Mobility Ratio`,
    map_data$`Rank - COVID-19 Incidence Rate`,
    map_data$`Rank - COVID-19 Hospital Admission Rate`,
    map_data$`Rank - COVID-19 Crude Mortality Rate`) %>%
    lapply(htmltools::HTML)

  leaflet(data = map_data) %>%
    addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
    addPolygons(
      fillColor = ~map_pal(`CCVI Category`),
      label = labels,
      weight = 2,
      opacity = 1,
      color = "white",
      dashArray = "3",
      fillOpacity = 0.7) %>%
    addLegend("bottomleft",
              pal = map_pal,
              values = ~`CCVI Category`,
              title = "CCVI Category",
              opacity = 1) %>%
    addResetMapButton() %>%
    addFullscreenControl()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ccvibycommunityarea
#| fig-cap: CCVI Scores by Community Area

# map CCVI category by community area
fx_map_ccvi(community_areas_ccvi, palette = "YlOrRd") # EDIT HERE

```

# Step 3. Evaluate CTA L ridership data before and during the COVID-19 pandemic
## Ridership by L station
The Regional Transportation Authority provides information on the location and performance of the three public transit operators within metropolitan Chicago, namely, PACE Suburban Bus, Chicago Transit Authority (CTA both bus and rail), and Metra commuter rail. The Chicago Data Portal also serves up daily boardings for CTA. For this exercise we focus specifically on CTA rail ridership using two datasets: (1) daily rail boardings for all L stations (`ridership_daily_boardings`, from the Chicago Data Portal); and (2) monthly boardings by L station (`ridership_attributes`, [downloaded from RTAMS](https://rtams.org/media/datasets/cta-ridership)).

## Create plots showing ridership trends over time
The following code uses the "plotly" package to create charts showing trends in total weekday boardings by month (@fig-railboardingsmonth) between January 1999 and November 2024 and weekday boardings by day (@fig-railboardingsdaily).

```{r}
#| label: define ridership plotting functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the ridership plotting functions"

# function for applying the layout shared by the exercise's plots: y axis title,
# horizontal legend below the plot, unified hover labels and an image download
# button that saves the plot as filename.png
fx_plot_layout <- function(p, y_title, filename, x_title = "") {
  p %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE,
           modeBarButtons = list(list("toImage", "resetScale2d")),
           toImageButtonOptions = list(filename = filename)) %>%
    layout(
      xaxis = list(title = x_title),
      yaxis = list(title = y_title),
      legend = list(
        font = list(size = 10),
        orientation = "h",
        xanchor = "center",
        x = 0.5, y = -0.1),
      hovermode = "x unified")
}

# function for plotting total boardings (all stations) by month; day_type is
# "Weekday", "Saturday" or "Sunday/Holiday"
fx_plot_ridership_by_month <- function(ridership_attributes, day_type = "Weekday") {
  ridership_by_month <- ridership_attributes %>%
    filter(day_type == !!day_type) %>%
    group_by(year_month) %>%
    summarise(rides_total = sum(rides_total), .groups = "drop")

  plot_ly(data = ridership_by_month,
          x = ~year_month,
          y = ~rides_total,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = "#080967", width = 0.5),
          name = 'Total boardings',
          hovertemplate = 'Rides: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = paste0("Total Rail Station Boardings (", day_type, ")"),
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_month")
}

# function for plotting daily rail boardings (all stations); day_type is "W"
# (weekday), "A" (Saturday) or "U" (Sunday/holiday)
fx_plot_daily_boardings <- function(ridership_daily_boardings, day_type = "W") {
  plot_ly(data = filter(ridership_daily_boardings, day_type == !!day_type),
          x = ~service_date,
          y = ~rail_boardings,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = "#9F1928", width = 0.5),
          name = 'Rail boardings',
          hovertemplate = 'Rail boardings: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = "Daily Rail Station Boardings",
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_day")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-railboardingsmonth
#| fig-cap: Total Weekday CTA L Rail Station Boardings by Month, Chicago, Illinois 1999-2024

# plot total weekday rail boardings per month
fx_plot_ridership_by_month(ridership_attributes, day_type = "Weekday")

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-railboardingsdaily
#| fig-cap: Weekday CTA L Rail Station Boardings by Day, Chicago, Illinois

# plot weekday rail boardings per day
fx_plot_daily_boardings(ridership_daily_boardings, day_type = "W")

```

## L stations by CCVI
The `rail_stations_ccvi` dataset joins each L station with the CCVI attributes of its community area, and the `rail_stations_ccvi_ridership` dataset adds monthly weekday boardings. These allow us to link trends in ridership by community area with CCVI scores and ranks. @fig-ccvibystation below tabulates L stations by line and CCVI.


## COVID-19 cases and deaths in Chicago
The Chicago data portal also makes available COVID-19 case and mortality data. Note that COVID-19 is no longer considered a notifiable disease, meaning that local health departments such as the Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH) no longer need to report COVID-19 cases to CDC. As a result, the city's COVID-19 data reporting ended in May 2024. These data (`covid19_cases_summary`) can be plotted to identify different waves of the pandemic then compared to trends in rail usage.

Compare trends in rail ridership (above) with COVID-19 trends reported by the city of Chicago shown in the plot below (@fig-covidcases7davg). *Create a customized version of the below plot by changing the layer from 7-day average deaths (i.e., "Deaths7d") to 7-day average cases (i.e., "Cases7d").*

```{r}
#| label: define COVID-19 plotting function
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the COVID-19 plotting function"

# function for plotting COVID-19 cases or deaths by date; layer is "Cases7d" or
# "Deaths7d" (7-day averages), "Cases" or "Deaths" (daily) or "Casescm" or
# "Deathscm" (cumulative)
fx_plot_covid <- function(covid19_cases_summary, layer = "Deaths7d") {
  layer_titles <- c(Cases7d = "COVID-19 Cases (7-day average)",
                    Deaths7d = "COVID-19 Deaths (7-day average)",
                    Cases = "COVID-19 Cases",
                    Deaths = "COVID-19 Deaths",
                    Casescm = "COVID-19 Cases (cumulative)",
                    Deathscm = "COVID-19 Deaths (cumulative)")
  title <- layer_titles[[layer]]

  plot_ly(data = filter(covid19_cases_summary, layer == !!layer),
          x = ~Date,
          y = ~value,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = "#9F1928", width = 0.5),
          name = title,
          hovertemplate = paste0(title, ': %{y:,}<extra></extra>')) %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = title,
                   filename = paste0("covid19_", tolower(layer), "_chicago"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-covidcases7davg
#| fig-cap: COVID-19 Deaths (rolling 7-day average) by Day, Chicago Illinois

# plot COVID-19 deaths (7-day average)
fx_plot_covid(covid19_cases_summary, layer = "Deaths7d") # EDIT HERE

```

# Step 4. Examine ridership by station characteristics
@fig-ridershipbyccvi plots ridership trends by CCVI category (i.e., Low, Medium, and High) whereas @fig-ridershipbyline shows ridership by CTA L Line.

```{r}
#| label: define ridership by station characteristics functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the ridership by CCVI and line plotting functions"

# CCVI category colors
pal_ccvi <- c(LOW = "#E2F11A", MEDIUM = "#E0A100", HIGH = "#9F1928")

# L line colors; names match station_line and the rail lines' COLOR column
pal_line <- c(Blue = "#3498db", Brown = "#964B00", Green = "#1e8449", Multi = "#424949",
              Orange = "#e67e22", Pink = "#f5b7b1", Purple = "#7d3c98", Red = "#e74c3c",
              Yellow = "#f4d03f")

# function for plotting weekday boardings by month and station CCVI category
fx_plot_ridership_by_ccvi <- function(rail_stations_ccvi_ridership) {
  ridership_by_ccvi <- rail_stations_ccvi_ridership %>%
    drop_na(`CCVI Category`) %>%
    group_by(year_month, `CCVI Category`) %>%
    summarise(rides_total = sum(rides_total), .groups = "drop")

  plot_ly(data = ridership_by_ccvi,
          x = ~year_month,
          y = ~rides_total,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          color = ~`CCVI Category`,
          colors = pal_ccvi,
          text = ~`CCVI Category`,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = "Total Weekday Rail Station Boardings",
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_ccvi")
}

# function for plotting weekday boardings by month and station line; lines is a
# list of line names (e.g., c("Blue", "Red")), all lines by default
fx_plot_ridership_by_line <- function(rail_stations_ccvi_ridership, lines = names(pal_line)) {
  ridership_by_line <- rail_stations_ccvi_ridership %>%
    filter(station_line %in% lines) %>%
    group_by(year_month, station_line) %>%
    summarise(rides_total = sum(rides_total), .groups = "drop")

  plot_ly(data = ridership_by_line,
          x = ~year_month,
          y = ~rides_total,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          color = ~station_line,
          colors = pal_line,
          text = ~station_line,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = "Total Weekday Rail Station Boardings",
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_line")
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Weekday Rail Boardings by CTA L Station CCVI Category, Chicago Illinois 1999-2024
```

# Step 5. Map of stations and ridership by L line
The final step is to create a custom map that displays changes in ridership by station for the rail lines you selected for further analysis. Stations shown in red have lost ridership between November 2019 and November 2024 (the latest month available). Hover over specific stations to display ridership numbers for the analyzed period as well as the net and percentage changes. Copy and paste the map into your presentation.

```{r}
#| label: define station change functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the station change functions"

# function for calculating the change in weekday boardings by station between
# two months (from and to, as "YYYY-MM-DD"); to is the latest month by default.
# Only stations on the selected lines are kept.
fx_station_change <- function(ridership_attributes, rail_stations, lines = names(pal_line),
                              from = "2019-11-01", to = NULL) {
  from <- as.Date(from)
  to <- if (is.null(to)) max(ridership_attributes$year_month) else as.Date(to)

  ridership_attributes %>%
    filter(day_type == "Weekday", year_month %in% c(from, to)) %>%
    group_by(station_id) %>%
    summarise(rides_from = sum(rides_total[year_month == from]),
              rides_to = sum(rides_total[year_month == to]),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(net_chg = rides_to - rides_from,
           pct_chg = net_chg / rides_from * 100,
           month_from = from,
           month_to = to) %>%
    filter(is.finite(pct_chg)) %>%
    inner_join(rail_stations %>%
                 select(station_id, station_name, station_line, comarea_id, comarea_name),
               by = "station_id") %>%
    st_as_sf() %>%
    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
    filter(station_line %in% lines)
}

# function for mapping the change in boardings by station (red: loss, blue: gain;
# larger circles for larger percentage changes) along with the selected lines
fx_map_station_change <- function(station_change, rail_lines, lines = names(pal_line)) {
  month_from <- format(station_change$month_from[1], "%b %Y")
  month_to <- format(station_change$month_to[1], "%b %Y")

  # station hover labels
  labels <- sprintf(
    "<strong>%s Station</strong><br/>
    <strong>%s Line</strong><br/>
    %s total: %s<br/>
    %s total: %s<br/>
    Net change: %s<br/>
    Percent change: %0.1f%%<br/>",
    station_change$station_name,
    station_change$station_line,
    month_from, format(station_change$rides_from, big.mark = ","),
    month_to, format(station_change$rides_to, big.mark = ","),
    format(station_change$net_chg, big.mark = ","),
    station_change$pct_chg) %>%
    lapply(htmltools::HTML)

  leaflet() %>%
    addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron, group = "Positron (minimal)") %>%
    addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "World Imagery (satellite)") %>%
    addPolylines(
      data = filter(rail_lines, COLOR %in% lines),
      weight = 2,
      opacity = 1,
      color = ~unname(pal_line[COLOR]),
      group = "Lines") %>%
    addCircleMarkers(
      data = station_change,
      radius = ~rescale(abs(pct_chg), to = c(3, 8)),
      color = ~if_else(pct_chg < 0, "red", "blue"),
      fillOpacity = 0.5,
      label = labels,
      group = "Stations") %>%
    addResetMapButton() %>%
    addFullscreenControl() %>%
    addLayersControl(
      baseGroups = c("Positron (minimal)", "World Imagery (satellite)"),
      overlayGroups = c("Lines", "Stations"),
      options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-selectstations
#| fig-cap: Change in Weekday Ridership by L Station, November 2019-2024

# calculate the change in weekday boardings by station for the selected lines
ridership_attributes_station <- fx_station_change(ridership_attributes, 
                                                  rail_stations, 
                                                  lines = a_station_line_list,
                                                  from = "2019-11-01")

# map the change in boardings by station and the selected lines
fx_map_station_change(ridership_attributes_station, rail_lines, lines = a_station_line_list)

```
